Edge cases to test:

  • k = 0 → the highest existing frequency.
  • All equal values → n.
  • Large k that can raise everything → n.

Complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort, O(n) for the window.

Medium 1888. Minimum Number of Flips to Make the Binary String Alternating Google Meta Microsoft String

Problem: You may rotate s (move the first character to the end) any number of times, then flip characters. Return the minimum number of flips to make s alternating.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "111000"
Output: 2
Explanation: Use the first operation two times to make s = "100011". Then, use the second operation on the third and sixth elements to make s = "101010".
Example 2
Input: s = "010"
Output: 0
Explanation: The string is already alternating.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s[i] is either '0' or '1'.

Hint 1

What do all rotations of s have in common with s + s?

Hint 2

Slide a window of length n over s + s, counting mismatches against both alternating patterns.

From brute force to the pattern: For each of the n rotations, counting mismatches is O(n): O(n²). In s + s consecutive rotations differ by one character in and one out, so the counts update in O(1).

Spot it: Every rotation of s is a window of length n in s + s. Compare each window with the two alternating patterns: the number of mismatches changes by at most one character in and one out as the window slides.

Why not another pattern? Rebuilding each rotation and counting mismatches is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Let t = s + s; every rotation of s is one window of length n in t.
  2. Slide a window of length n over t, keeping mismatch counts against both patterns 0101… and 1010….
  3. Each full window gives a candidate: the smaller of the two counts.
class Solution:
    def minFlips(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        t = s + s  # every rotation is a window of length n
        diff_a = 0  # mismatches against "0101..."
        diff_b = 0  # mismatches against "1010..."
        best = n
        for i in range(len(t)):
            expect_a = "0" if i % 2 == 0 else "1"
            if t[i] != expect_a:
                diff_a = diff_a + 1
            else:
                diff_b = diff_b + 1  # matching "0101..." means mismatching "1010..."
            if i >= n:  # the character at i - n leaves the window
                old = t[i - n]
                old_expect_a = "0" if (i - n) % 2 == 0 else "1"
                if old != old_expect_a:
                    diff_a = diff_a - 1
                else:
                    diff_b = diff_b - 1
            if i >= n - 1:
                best = min(best, diff_a, diff_b)  # a full rotation is in the window
        return best
function minFlips(s: string): number {
    const n = s.length;
    const t = s + s;  // every rotation is a window of length n
    let diffA = 0;  // mismatches against "0101..."
    let diffB = 0;  // mismatches against "1010..."
    let best = n;
    for (let i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
        const expectA = i % 2 === 0 ? "0" : "1";
        if (t[i] !== expectA) {
            diffA = diffA + 1;
        } else {
            diffB = diffB + 1;  // matching "0101..." means mismatching "1010..."
        }
        if (i >= n) {  // the character at i - n leaves the window
            const old = t[i - n];
            const oldExpectA = (i - n) % 2 === 0 ? "0" : "1";
            if (old !== oldExpectA) {
                diffA = diffA - 1;
            } else {
                diffB = diffB - 1;
            }
        }
        if (i >= n - 1) {
            best = Math.min(best, diffA, diffB);  // a full rotation is in the window
        }
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int minFlips(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        String t = s + s;  // every rotation is a window of length n
        int diffA = 0;  // mismatches against "0101..."
        int diffB = 0;  // mismatches against "1010..."
        int best = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < t.length(); i++) {
            char expectA = i % 2 == 0 ? '0' : '1';
            if (t.charAt(i) != expectA) {
                diffA = diffA + 1;
            } else {
                diffB = diffB + 1;  // matching "0101..." means mismatching "1010..."
            }
            if (i >= n) {  // the character at i - n leaves the window
                char old = t.charAt(i - n);
                char oldExpectA = (i - n) % 2 == 0 ? '0' : '1';
                if (old != oldExpectA) {
                    diffA = diffA - 1;
                } else {
                    diffB = diffB - 1;
                }
            }
            if (i >= n - 1) {
                best = Math.min(best, Math.min(diffA, diffB));  // a full rotation is in the window
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. t = s + s: rotating by r gives t[r : r + n].
  2. The patterns are fixed to positions in t; a window starting at an odd index simply uses them shifted, which is why both patterns are tracked.
  3. Each character either matches pattern A or pattern B, so exactly one of the two counters goes up.
  4. When the window is longer than n, the character leaving it is removed from whichever counter it was in.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already alternating → 0.
  • Odd length (rotation actually helps), e.g. "111000" → 2.
  • A single character → 0.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for s + s.

Medium 2461. Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K Google Amazon ArrayHash Map

Problem: Among subarrays of length k whose elements are all distinct, return the maximum sum (0 if none).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,5,4,2,9,9,9], k = 3
Output: 15
Explanation: The subarrays of nums with length 3 are: - [1,5,4] which meets the requirements and has a sum of 10. - [5,4,2] which meets the requirements and has a sum of 11. - [4,2,9] which meets the requirements and has a sum of 15. - [2,9,9] which does not meet the requirements because the element 9 is repeated. - [9,9,9] which does not meet the requirements because the element 9 is repeated. We return 15 because it is the maximum subarray sum of all the subarrays that meet the conditions
Example 2
Input: nums = [4,4,4], k = 3
Output: 0
Explanation: The subarrays of nums with length 3 are: - [4,4,4] which does not meet the requirements because the element 4 is repeated. We return 0 because no subarrays meet the conditions.

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵

Hint 1

All windows have length k. How can you tell if a window has no duplicates?

Hint 2

Keep a count map of the window; it has no duplicates exactly when it has k keys.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking each window with a fresh set is O(n · k). A count map updated as the window slides is O(1) per step.

Spot it: Fixed-length windows (k) with a property of their contents (all distinct): slide the window and keep counts of the values inside.

Why not another pattern? Rebuilding a set for every window is O(n · k). A count map updated by one add and one remove per slide is O(1) per step.

Approach:

  1. Slide a window of size k, keeping count of each value and the window sum.
  2. When a value's count drops to 0, delete it, so len(count) is the number of distinct values.
  3. If len(count) == k, the window is valid: update the best sum.
class Solution:
    def maximumSubarraySum(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        count = {}  # value -> occurrences inside the window
        window_sum = 0
        best = 0
        for right in range(len(nums)):
            x = nums[right]
            count[x] = count.get(x, 0) + 1
            window_sum = window_sum + x
            if right >= k:
                old = nums[right - k]  # the element leaving the window
                count[old] = count[old] - 1
                if count[old] == 0:
                    del count[old]
                window_sum = window_sum - old
            if right >= k - 1 and len(count) == k:
                best = max(best, window_sum)  # all k values are distinct
        return best
function maximumSubarraySum(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    const count = new Map<number, number>();  // value -> occurrences inside the window
    let windowSum = 0;
    let best = 0;
    for (let right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        const x = nums[right];
        count.set(x, (count.get(x) ?? 0) + 1);
        windowSum = windowSum + x;
        if (right >= k) {
            const old = nums[right - k];  // the element leaving the window
            count.set(old, count.get(old)! - 1);
            if (count.get(old) === 0) {
                count.delete(old);
            }
            windowSum = windowSum - old;
        }
        if (right >= k - 1 && count.size === k) {
            best = Math.max(best, windowSum);  // all k values are distinct
        }
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public long maximumSubarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();  // value -> occurrences inside the window
        long windowSum = 0;
        long best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            int x = nums[right];
            count.put(x, count.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1);
            windowSum = windowSum + x;
            if (right >= k) {
                int old = nums[right - k];  // the element leaving the window
                count.put(old, count.get(old) - 1);
                if (count.get(old) == 0) {
                    count.remove(old);
                }
                windowSum = windowSum - old;
            }
            if (right >= k - 1 && count.size() == k) {
                best = Math.max(best, windowSum);  // all k values are distinct
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Add the entering element to count and to the sum.
  2. Once the window is longer than k, remove nums[right - k]; deleting zero counts keeps len(count) equal to the number of distinct values.
  3. A full window with k distinct keys has no duplicates.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No valid window → 0.
  • k = 1 → the maximum element.
  • A duplicate that enters and leaves the window.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(k) space.

Medium 2958. Length of Longest Subarray With at Most K Frequency Google Amazon ArrayHash Map

Problem: Return the length of the longest subarray in which every value occurs at most k times.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,1,2,3,1,2], k = 2
Output: 6
Explanation: The longest possible good subarray is [1,2,3,1,2,3] since the values 1, 2, and 3 occur at most twice in this subarray. Note that the subarrays [2,3,1,2,3,1] and [3,1,2,3,1,2] are also good. It can be shown that there are no good subarrays with length more than 6.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,1,2,1,2,1,2], k = 1
Output: 2
Explanation: The longest possible good subarray is [1,2] since the values 1 and 2 occur at most once in this subarray. Note that the subarray [2,1] is also good. It can be shown that there are no good subarrays with length more than 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length

Hint 1

When you add a new element to a valid window, which value could break the rule?

Hint 2

Shrink from the left until that value's count is at most k.

From brute force to the pattern: Counting frequencies for every subarray is O(n²). The window keeps counts incrementally and each index moves at most twice: O(n).

Spot it: Longest contiguous window satisfying a frequency limit: a variable sliding window. The only value that can exceed k after adding nums[right] is nums[right] itself, so shrink until its count is back to k.

Why not another pattern? Checking every subarray is O(n²). Binary search on the length with a check per length is O(n log n); the window is linear.

Approach:

  1. Add nums[right] to the counts.
  2. While its count exceeds k, remove nums[left] and move left right.
  3. Track the longest window.
class Solution:
    def maxSubarrayLength(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        count = {}
        left = 0
        best = 0
        for right in range(len(nums)):
            x = nums[right]
            count[x] = count.get(x, 0) + 1
            while count[x] > k:
                count[nums[left]] = count[nums[left]] - 1  # shrink until x is allowed again
                left = left + 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best
function maxSubarrayLength(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    const count = new Map<number, number>();
    let left = 0;
    let best = 0;
    for (let right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        const x = nums[right];
        count.set(x, (count.get(x) ?? 0) + 1);
        while (count.get(x)! > k) {
            count.set(nums[left], count.get(nums[left])! - 1);  // shrink until x is allowed again
            left = left + 1;
        }
        best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxSubarrayLength(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
        int left = 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            int x = nums[right];
            count.put(x, count.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1);
            while (count.get(x) > k) {
                count.put(nums[left], count.get(nums[left]) - 1);  // shrink until x is allowed again
                left = left + 1;
            }
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. count tracks frequencies inside the window.
  2. Only x can have just gone over the limit, so the loop shrinks until count[x] ≤ k.
  3. right - left + 1 is the current valid window length.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k ≥ n → the whole array.
  • All elements equal → k.
  • k = 1 → the longest subarray of distinct values.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 3356. Zero Array Transformation II Google Array

Problem: Query [l, r, val] lets you decrement each element in l..r by up to val. Return the smallest k such that the first k queries can turn nums into all zeros, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [2,0,2], queries = [[0,2,1],[0,2,1],[1,1,3]]
Output: 2
Explanation: For i = 0 (l = 0, r = 2, val = 1): Decrement values at indices [0, 1, 2] by [1, 0, 1] respectively. The array will become [1, 0, 1]. For i = 1 (l = 0, r = 2, val = 1): Decrement values at indices [0, 1, 2] by [1, 0, 1] respectively. The array will become [0, 0, 0], which is a Zero Array. Therefore, the minimum value of k is 2.
Example 2
Input: nums = [4,3,2,1], queries = [[1,3,2],[0,2,1]]
Output: -1
Explanation: For i = 0 (l = 1, r = 3, val = 2): Decrement values at indices [1, 2, 3] by [2, 2, 1] respectively. The array will become [4, 1, 0, 0]. For i = 1 (l = 0, r = 2, val = 1): Decrement values at indices [0, 1, 2] by [1, 1, 0] respectively. The array will become [3, 0, 0, 0], which is not a Zero Array.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 5 * 10⁵ · 1 ≤ queries.length ≤ 10⁵ · queries[i].length == 3 · 0 ≤ li ≤ ri < nums.length · 1 ≤ vali ≤ 5

Hint 1

Process the array from left to right. When do you need another query?

Hint 2

Keep the available decrement at index i with a difference array, and add queries one by one until it reaches nums[i].

From brute force to the pattern: Trying each k and simulating all k queries is O(q · (n + q)). Because the first k queries are always used in order, one left-to-right sweep that pulls queries only when needed finds the minimum k in O(n + q).

Spot it: Walk the array left to right keeping how much decrement is available at the current index. Whenever it's not enough, pull in the next query; queries only ever move forward, so this is a two-pointer sweep with a difference array for the ranges.

Why not another pattern? Binary search on k with a difference-array check per guess is O((n + q) log q) and also fine; the sweep avoids the log factor.

Approach:

  1. diff records where each applied query's decrement starts and stops; power is the running sum at index i.
  2. At index i, add diff[i] to power.
  3. While power < nums[i]: apply query k. If it covers i, it contributes now (power += val) and stops after r; if it starts later, record it in diff. If no queries are left, return −1.
  4. After the sweep, k is the answer.
class Solution:
    def minZeroArray(self, nums: List[int], queries: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        diff = [0] * (n + 1)  # decrement starting/stopping at each index
        power = 0  # total decrement available at the current index
        k = 0  # number of queries used so far
        for i in range(n):
            power = power + diff[i]
            while power < nums[i]:
                if k == len(queries):
                    return -1  # every query used and nums[i] still can't reach 0
                l, r, val = queries[k]
                k = k + 1
                if r < i:
                    continue  # this query only covers indices we've already handled
                start = max(l, i)
                if start == i:
                    power = power + val  # covers i right now
                else:
                    diff[start] = diff[start] + val  # starts later
                diff[r + 1] = diff[r + 1] - val  # stops after r
        return k
function minZeroArray(nums: number[], queries: number[][]): number {
    const n = nums.length;
    const diff: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);  // decrement starting/stopping at each index
    let power = 0;  // total decrement available at the current index
    let k = 0;  // number of queries used so far
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        power = power + diff[i];
        while (power < nums[i]) {
            if (k === queries.length) {
                return -1;  // every query used and nums[i] still can't reach 0
            }
            const [l, r, val] = queries[k];
            k = k + 1;
            if (r < i) {
                continue;  // this query only covers indices we've already handled
            }
            const start = Math.max(l, i);
            if (start === i) {
                power = power + val;  // covers i right now
            } else {
                diff[start] = diff[start] + val;  // starts later
            }
            diff[r + 1] = diff[r + 1] - val;  // stops after r
        }
    }
    return k;
}
class Solution {
    public int minZeroArray(int[] nums, int[][] queries) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] diff = new int[n + 1];  // decrement starting/stopping at each index
        int power = 0;  // total decrement available at the current index
        int k = 0;  // number of queries used so far
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            power = power + diff[i];
            while (power < nums[i]) {
                if (k == queries.length) {
                    return -1;  // every query used and nums[i] still can't reach 0
                }
                int l = queries[k][0], r = queries[k][1], val = queries[k][2];
                k = k + 1;
                if (r < i) {
                    continue;  // this query only covers indices we've already handled
                }
                int start = Math.max(l, i);
                if (start == i) {
                    power = power + val;  // covers i right now
                } else {
                    diff[start] = diff[start] + val;  // starts later
                }
                diff[r + 1] = diff[r + 1] - val;  // stops after r
            }
        }
        return k;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. power is the sum of val over the applied queries that cover index i (a running prefix sum of diff).
  2. The while pulls in queries in order only when needed, so k ends as small as possible.
  3. A query that ends before i is still "processed" (it counts toward k) but can't help anymore.
  4. Queries starting at or before i add to power immediately; later ones are scheduled in diff. All of them stop at r + 1.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already all zeros → 0.
  • Not enough total decrement → −1.
  • A query that ends before the index that needs it (it still counts toward k).

Complexity: O(n + q) time, O(n) space.

Medium 1456. Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length Meta Microsoft String

Problem: Return the maximum number of vowels in any substring of length k.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abciiidef", k = 3
Output: 3
Explanation: The substring "iii" contains 3 vowel letters.
Example 2
Input: s = "aeiou", k = 2
Output: 2
Explanation: Any substring of length 2 contains 2 vowels.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s consists of lowercase English letters. · 1 ≤ k ≤ s.length

Hint 1

All windows have length k.

Hint 2

Update the count as the window slides instead of recounting.

From brute force to the pattern: Recounting each window is O(nk); sliding is O(n).

Spot it: Every window has the same length → fixed-size sliding window: one character enters and one leaves per step.

Why not another pattern? Recounting each window is O(n · k).

Approach:

  1. Count vowels in the first k characters.
  2. Slide: +1 if s[i] is a vowel, −1 if s[i − k] was.
  3. Track the maximum.
class Solution:
    def maxVowels(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        vowels = set("aeiou")
        count = sum(ch in vowels for ch in s[:k])  # first window
        best = count
        for i in range(k, len(s)):
            count += (s[i] in vowels) - (s[i - k] in vowels)  # one enters, one leaves
            best = max(best, count)
        return best
function maxVowels(s: string, k: number): number {
    const vowels = new Set("aeiou");
    let count = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        count += vowels.has(s[i]) ? 1 : 0;  // first window
    }
    let best = count;
    for (let i = k; i < s.length; i++) {
        count += (vowels.has(s[i]) ? 1 : 0) - (vowels.has(s[i - k]) ? 1 : 0);  // one enters, one leaves
        best = Math.max(best, count);
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxVowels(String s, int k) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            count += isVowel(s.charAt(i)) ? 1 : 0;  // first window
        }
        int best = count;
        for (int i = k; i < s.length(); i++) {
            count += (isVowel(s.charAt(i)) ? 1 : 0) - (isVowel(s.charAt(i - k)) ? 1 : 0);  // one enters, one leaves
            best = Math.max(best, count);
        }
        return best;
    }

    private boolean isVowel(char ch) {
        return "aeiou".indexOf(ch) >= 0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Booleans add as 0/1 in Python.
  2. Each step costs O(1).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k == len(s).
  • No vowels → 0.
  • All vowels → k.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 187. Repeated DNA Sequences Amazon Microsoft StringHash Set

Problem: Return every 10-letter substring that occurs more than once.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "AAAAACCCCCAAAAACCCCCCAAAAAGGGTTT"
Output: ["AAAAACCCCC","CCCCCAAAAA"]
Example 2
Input: s = "AAAAAAAAAAAAA"
Output: ["AAAAAAAAAA"]

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s[i] is either 'A', 'C', 'G', or 'T'.

Hint 1

Look at every substring of length 10.

Hint 2

Remember which ones you've seen.

From brute force to the pattern: Pairwise comparison is O(n²); a set of windows is linear.

Spot it: Fixed-size sliding window of 10 characters with a hash set of windows seen so far.

Why not another pattern? Comparing every pair of windows is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. For each start i: w = s[i:i + 10].
  2. If w is in seen, add it to repeated; else add it to seen.
class Solution:
    def findRepeatedDnaSequences(self, s: str) -> List[str]:
        seen, repeated = set(), set()
        for i in range(len(s) - 9):
            window = s[i:i + 10]
            if window in seen:
                repeated.add(window)  # second (or later) occurrence
            else:
                seen.add(window)
        return list(repeated)
function findRepeatedDnaSequences(s: string): string[] {
    const seen = new Set<string>();
    const repeated = new Set<string>();
    for (let i = 0; i + 10 <= s.length; i++) {
        const window = s.substring(i, i + 10);
        if (seen.has(window)) {
            repeated.add(window);  // second (or later) occurrence
        } else {
            seen.add(window);
        }
    }
    return [...repeated];
}
class Solution {
    public List<String> findRepeatedDnaSequences(String s) {
        Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
        Set<String> repeated = new HashSet<>();
        for (int i = 0; i + 10 <= s.length(); i++) {
            String window = s.substring(i, i + 10);
            if (seen.contains(window)) {
                repeated.add(window);  // second (or later) occurrence
            } else {
                seen.add(window);
            }
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(repeated);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A set for repeats avoids listing the same sequence twice.
  2. A 2-bit encoding per letter (rolling hash in 20 bits) avoids slicing, but slicing 10 letters is cheap.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Shorter than 10 → [].
  • Overlapping repeats (AAAAAAAAAAA).
  • Same sequence many times (listed once).

Complexity: O(10n) time, O(10n) space.

Medium 1151. Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together Amazon Array

Problem: Return the minimum swaps (of any two elements) to group all 1s together.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: data = [1,0,1,0,1]
Output: 1
Explanation: Swap the middle 0 with an end 1, e.g. [0,0,1,1,1].
Example 2
Input: data = [0,0,0,1,0]
Output: 0
Example 3
Input: data = [1,0,1,0,1,0,0,1,1,0,1]
Output: 3

Constraints: 1 ≤ data.length ≤ 10⁵ · data[i] is either 0 or 1

Hint 1

How long is the final block of ones?

Hint 2

Which window of that length needs the fewest swaps?

From brute force to the pattern: Counting each window from scratch is O(nm); sliding is O(n).

Spot it: All m ones end up in some window of length m. Every 0 inside that window needs one swap, so find the window with the most ones: a fixed-size sliding window.

Why not another pattern? Trying every target window and counting from scratch is O(n · m).

Approach:

  1. m = sum(data).
  2. Slide a window of size m, tracking its ones.
  3. Answer m − max ones in a window.
class Solution:
    def minSwaps(self, data: List[int]) -> int:
        m = sum(data)  # the group's final length
        if m <= 1:
            return 0
        ones = best = sum(data[:m])
        for i in range(m, len(data)):
            ones += data[i] - data[i - m]  # slide by one
            best = max(best, ones)
        return m - best  # each 0 in the best window needs one swap
function minSwaps(data: number[]): number {
    let m = 0;  // the group's final length
    for (const x of data) {
        m = m + x;
    }
    if (m <= 1) {
        return 0;
    }
    let ones = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < m; i++) {
        ones = ones + data[i];
    }
    let best = ones;
    for (let i = m; i < data.length; i++) {
        ones += data[i] - data[i - m];  // slide by one
        best = Math.max(best, ones);
    }
    return m - best;  // each 0 in the best window needs one swap
}
class Solution {
    public int minSwaps(int[] data) {
        int m = 0;  // the group's final length
        for (int x : data) {
            m = m + x;
        }
        if (m <= 1) {
            return 0;
        }
        int ones = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            ones = ones + data[i];
        }
        int best = ones;
        for (int i = m; i < data.length; i++) {
            ones += data[i] - data[i - m];  // slide by one
            best = Math.max(best, ones);
        }
        return m - best;  // each 0 in the best window needs one swap
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Any swap can bring one outside 1 into the window, replacing a 0.
  2. The window with the most ones needs the fewest swaps.

Edge cases to test:

  • No ones or one one → 0.
  • All ones → 0.
  • Ones at both ends.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1438. Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit Amazon ArrayDeque

Problem: Return the longest subarray in which every pair differs by at most limit.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [8,2,4,7], limit = 4
Output: 2
Explanation: Checking every subarray, where the absolute difference is taken over all pairs of its elements: [8] with maximum absolute diff |8-8| = 0 <= 4. [8,2] with maximum absolute diff |8-2| = 6 > 4. [8,2,4] with maximum absolute diff |8-2| = 6 > 4. [8,2,4,7] with maximum absolute diff |8-2| = 6 > 4. [2] with maximum absolute diff |2-2| = 0 <= 4. [2,4] with maximum absolute diff |4-2| = 2 <= 4. [2,4,7] with maximum absolute diff |7-2| = 5 > 4. Note that the pair (2, 7) is not adjacent, but it is still compared. [4] with maximum absolute diff |4-4| = 0 <= 4. [4,7] with maximum absolute diff |7-4| = 3 <= 4. [7] with maximum absolute diff |7-7| = 0 <= 4. Therefore, the size of the longest subarray is 2.
Example 2
Input: nums = [10,1,2,4,7,2], limit = 5
Output: 4
Explanation: The subarray [2,4,7,2] is valid because every pair of its elements differs by at most 5, the largest being |7-2| = 5. It cannot be extended to the left, since [1,2,4,7,2] contains the pair (1, 7) with |7-1| = 6 > 5. Therefore, the size of the longest subarray is 4.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 0 ≤ limit ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

The condition only depends on the window's max and min.

Hint 2

Maintain both with monotonic deques while sliding.

From brute force to the pattern: All subarrays: O(n²); a sorted structure: O(n log n); two deques: O(n).

Spot it: "Longest subarray with a condition that only gets worse as it grows" → sliding window. The condition is max − min ≤ limit, so keep the window max and min in two monotonic deques.

Why not another pattern? Recomputing max and min for every window is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. maxq decreasing, minq increasing (indices).
  2. Add right; while max − min > limit, move left and drop deque fronts that fall out.
  3. Track the longest window.
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def longestSubarray(self, nums: List[int], limit: int) -> int:
        maxq, minq = deque(), deque()  # indices; values decreasing / increasing
        left = best = 0
        for right, x in enumerate(nums):
            while maxq and nums[maxq[-1]] <= x:
                maxq.pop()
            maxq.append(right)
            while minq and nums[minq[-1]] >= x:
                minq.pop()
            minq.append(right)
            while nums[maxq[0]] - nums[minq[0]] > limit:
                left += 1  # shrink until the window is valid
                if maxq[0] < left:
                    maxq.popleft()
                if minq[0] < left:
                    minq.popleft()
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best
function longestSubarray(nums: number[], limit: number): number {
    // indices; values decreasing / increasing. Arrays with head indexes act as deques.
    const maxq: number[] = [];
    const minq: number[] = [];
    let maxHead = 0;
    let minHead = 0;
    let left = 0;
    let best = 0;
    for (let right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        const x = nums[right];
        while (maxq.length > maxHead && nums[maxq[maxq.length - 1]] <= x) {
            maxq.pop();
        }
        maxq.push(right);
        while (minq.length > minHead && nums[minq[minq.length - 1]] >= x) {
            minq.pop();
        }
        minq.push(right);
        while (nums[maxq[maxHead]] - nums[minq[minHead]] > limit) {
            left += 1;  // shrink until the window is valid
            if (maxq[maxHead] < left) {
                maxHead++;
            }
            if (minq[minHead] < left) {
                minHead++;
            }
        }
        best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int longestSubarray(int[] nums, int limit) {
        Deque<Integer> maxq = new ArrayDeque<>();  // indices; values decreasing
        Deque<Integer> minq = new ArrayDeque<>();  // indices; values increasing
        int left = 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            int x = nums[right];
            while (!maxq.isEmpty() && nums[maxq.peekLast()] <= x) {
                maxq.pollLast();
            }
            maxq.addLast(right);
            while (!minq.isEmpty() && nums[minq.peekLast()] >= x) {
                minq.pollLast();
            }
            minq.addLast(right);
            while (nums[maxq.peekFirst()] - nums[minq.peekFirst()] > limit) {
                left += 1;  // shrink until the window is valid
                if (maxq.peekFirst() < left) {
                    maxq.pollFirst();
                }
                if (minq.peekFirst() < left) {
                    minq.pollFirst();
                }
            }
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The deque fronts are always the current window's max and min.
  2. Each index enters and leaves each deque once.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • limit = 0 (runs of equal values).
  • All equal.
  • Large swings.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 2271. Maximum White Tiles Covered by a Carpet Amazon Array

Problem: Tile ranges [l, r] are white (non-overlapping). Place one carpet of length carpetLen. Return the most white tiles covered.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: tiles = [[1,5],[10,11],[12,18],[20,25],[30,32]], carpetLen = 10
Output: 9
Explanation: Place the carpet starting on tile 10. It covers 9 white tiles, so we return 9. Note that there may be other places where the carpet covers 9 white tiles. It can be shown that the carpet cannot cover more than 9 white tiles.
Example 2
Input: tiles = [[10,11],[1,1]], carpetLen = 2
Output: 2
Explanation: Place the carpet starting on tile 10. It covers 2 white tiles, so we return 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ tiles.length ≤ 5 * 10⁴ · tiles[i].length == 2 · 1 ≤ li ≤ ri ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ carpetLen ≤ 10⁹ · The tiles are non-overlapping.

Hint 1

Where should the carpet start?

Hint 2

Slide over the tile ranges, counting full ranges and one partial range.

From brute force to the pattern: Every start coordinate is infeasible; starting at range ends gives O(n log n).

Spot it: A best carpet can start at some range's left end (shifting it right to one never loses tiles). Then it's a sliding window over ranges: add fully covered ranges, plus the partly covered one.

Why not another pattern? Trying every start position is impossible with coordinates up to 10⁹.

Approach:

  1. Sort ranges.
  2. For each start range i: end = l_i + len − 1; advance j over ranges ending ≤ end, summing their lengths.
  3. Add the partial overlap of range j; then remove range i.
class Solution:
    def maximumWhiteTiles(self, tiles: List[List[int]], carpetLen: int) -> int:
        tiles = sorted(tiles)
        best = covered = 0
        j = 0
        for i, (l, r) in enumerate(tiles):
            end = l + carpetLen - 1
            while j < len(tiles) and tiles[j][1] <= end:
                covered += tiles[j][1] - tiles[j][0] + 1  # fully under the carpet
                j += 1
            partial = max(0, end - tiles[j][0] + 1) if j < len(tiles) else 0
            best = max(best, covered + partial)
            if j > i:
                covered -= r - l + 1  # the carpet moves past range i
            else:
                j = i + 1  # range i itself was only partly covered
        return best
function maximumWhiteTiles(tiles: number[][], carpetLen: number): number {
    tiles = [...tiles].sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
    let best = 0;
    let covered = 0;
    let j = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < tiles.length; i++) {
        const [l, r] = tiles[i];
        const end = l + carpetLen - 1;
        while (j < tiles.length && tiles[j][1] <= end) {
            covered += tiles[j][1] - tiles[j][0] + 1;  // fully under the carpet
            j += 1;
        }
        const partial = j < tiles.length ? Math.max(0, end - tiles[j][0] + 1) : 0;
        best = Math.max(best, covered + partial);
        if (j > i) {
            covered -= r - l + 1;  // the carpet moves past range i
        } else {
            j = i + 1;  // range i itself was only partly covered
        }
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int maximumWhiteTiles(int[][] tiles, int carpetLen) {
        tiles = tiles.clone();
        Arrays.sort(tiles, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
        int best = 0;
        int covered = 0;
        int j = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < tiles.length; i++) {
            int l = tiles[i][0], r = tiles[i][1];
            int end = l + carpetLen - 1;
            while (j < tiles.length && tiles[j][1] <= end) {
                covered += tiles[j][1] - tiles[j][0] + 1;  // fully under the carpet
                j += 1;
            }
            int partial = j < tiles.length ? Math.max(0, end - tiles[j][0] + 1) : 0;
            best = Math.max(best, covered + partial);
            if (j > i) {
                covered -= r - l + 1;  // the carpet moves past range i
            } else {
                j = i + 1;  // range i itself was only partly covered
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Starting at a range's left end is never worse than starting in a gap or partway into a range.
  2. When the carpet is shorter than range i, j stays at i, the partial covers carpetLen, and nothing is subtracted.

  • Carpet longer than all tiles.
  • Carpet shorter than one range.
  • Big gaps.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

Medium 2653. Sliding Subarray Beauty Amazon Array

Problem: For each window of size k, return its x-th smallest negative number, or 0 if there are fewer than x negatives.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,-1,-3,-2,3], k = 3, x = 2
Output: [-1,-2,-2]
Explanation: There are 3 subarrays with size k = 3. The first subarray is [1, -1, -3] and the 2nd smallest negative integer is -1. The second subarray is [-1, -3, -2] and the 2nd smallest negative integer is -2. The third subarray is [-3, -2, 3] and the 2nd smallest negative integer is -2.
Example 2
Input: nums = [-1,-2,-3,-4,-5], k = 2, x = 2
Output: [-1,-2,-3,-4]
Explanation: There are 4 subarrays with size k = 2. For [-1, -2], the 2nd smallest negative integer is -1. For [-2, -3], the 2nd smallest negative integer is -2. For [-3, -4], the 2nd smallest negative integer is -3. For [-4, -5], the 2nd smallest negative integer is -4.

Constraints: n == nums.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ k ≤ n · 1 ≤ x ≤ k · -50 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 50

Hint 1

The values are small. How can you find the x-th smallest quickly?

Hint 2

Keep a count of each negative value in the window.

From brute force to the pattern: Sorting every window is O(nk log k); counting is O(50n).

Spot it: Fixed-size sliding window with a tiny value range: a count array over −50..−1 lets you find the x-th smallest negative in 50 steps.

Why not another pattern? Sorting each window is O(n · k log k).

Approach:

  1. count[v + 50] for negatives in the window.
  2. Slide: add the new value, remove the old one.
  3. Walk counts from −50 upward until x values are passed.
class Solution:
    def getSubarrayBeauty(self, nums: List[int], k: int, x: int) -> List[int]:
        count = [0] * 50  # count[v + 50] for v in -50..-1
        result = []
        for i, v in enumerate(nums):
            if v < 0:
                count[v + 50] += 1
            if i >= k and nums[i - k] < 0:
                count[nums[i - k] + 50] -= 1  # leaves the window
            if i >= k - 1:
                seen = 0
                beauty = 0
                for j in range(50):  # smallest negatives first
                    seen += count[j]
                    if seen >= x:
                        beauty = j - 50
                        break
                result.append(beauty)
        return result
function getSubarrayBeauty(nums: number[], k: number, x: number): number[] {
    const count: number[] = new Array(50).fill(0);  // count[v + 50] for v in -50..-1
    const result: number[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        const v = nums[i];
        if (v < 0) {
            count[v + 50] += 1;
        }
        if (i >= k && nums[i - k] < 0) {
            count[nums[i - k] + 50] -= 1;  // leaves the window
        }
        if (i >= k - 1) {
            let seen = 0;
            let beauty = 0;
            for (let j = 0; j < 50; j++) {  // smallest negatives first
                seen += count[j];
                if (seen >= x) {
                    beauty = j - 50;
                    break;
                }
            }
            result.push(beauty);
        }
    }
    return result;
}
class Solution {
    public int[] getSubarrayBeauty(int[] nums, int k, int x) {
        int[] count = new int[50];  // count[v + 50] for v in -50..-1
        int[] result = new int[nums.length - k + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int v = nums[i];
            if (v < 0) {
                count[v + 50] += 1;
            }
            if (i >= k && nums[i - k] < 0) {
                count[nums[i - k] + 50] -= 1;  // leaves the window
            }
            if (i >= k - 1) {
                int seen = 0;
                int beauty = 0;
                for (int j = 0; j < 50; j++) {  // smallest negatives first
                    seen += count[j];
                    if (seen >= x) {
                        beauty = j - 50;
                        break;
                    }
                }
                result[i - k + 1] = beauty;
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Only negatives matter, and there are just 50 possible values.
  2. Walking the counts in increasing value finds the x-th smallest.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Fewer than x negatives → 0.
  • All negative.
  • k = 1.

Complexity: O(50 · n) time, O(1) extra space.

Medium 2762. Continuous Subarrays Amazon ArrayDeque

Problem: Count subarrays where every pair of elements differs by at most 2.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [5,4,2,4]
Output: 8
Explanation: Continuous subarray of size 1: [5], [4], [2], [4]. Continuous subarray of size 2: [5,4], [4,2], [2,4]. Continuous subarray of size 3: [4,2,4]. There are no subarrys of size 4. Total continuous subarrays = 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. It can be shown that there are no more continuous subarrays.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,3]
Output: 6
Explanation: Continuous subarray of size 1: [1], [2], [3]. Continuous subarray of size 2: [1,2], [2,3]. Continuous subarray of size 3: [1,2,3]. Total continuous subarrays = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

For each right end, which left ends give a valid subarray?

Hint 2

Track the window's max and min with monotonic deques.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking all subarrays is O(n²); the counting window is O(n).

Spot it: Same window as the previous problem (max − min ≤ limit with monotonic deques), but count: each valid window [left, right] adds right − left + 1 subarrays ending at right.

Why not another pattern? Checking every subarray is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Slide with max/min deques; shrink while max − min > 2.
  2. Add right − left + 1 for each right.
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def continuousSubarrays(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        maxq, minq = deque(), deque()
        left = count = 0
        for right, x in enumerate(nums):
            while maxq and nums[maxq[-1]] <= x:
                maxq.pop()
            maxq.append(right)
            while minq and nums[minq[-1]] >= x:
                minq.pop()
            minq.append(right)
            while nums[maxq[0]] - nums[minq[0]] > 2:
                left += 1
                if maxq[0] < left:
                    maxq.popleft()
                if minq[0] < left:
                    minq.popleft()
            count += right - left + 1  # every start in [left, right] works
        return count
function continuousSubarrays(nums: number[]): number {
    // indices; values decreasing / increasing. Arrays with head indexes act as deques.
    const maxq: number[] = [];
    const minq: number[] = [];
    let maxHead = 0;
    let minHead = 0;
    let left = 0;
    let count = 0;
    for (let right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        const x = nums[right];
        while (maxq.length > maxHead && nums[maxq[maxq.length - 1]] <= x) {
            maxq.pop();
        }
        maxq.push(right);
        while (minq.length > minHead && nums[minq[minq.length - 1]] >= x) {
            minq.pop();
        }
        minq.push(right);
        while (nums[maxq[maxHead]] - nums[minq[minHead]] > 2) {
            left += 1;
            if (maxq[maxHead] < left) {
                maxHead++;
            }
            if (minq[minHead] < left) {
                minHead++;
            }
        }
        count += right - left + 1;  // every start in [left, right] works
    }
    return count;
}
class Solution {
    public long continuousSubarrays(int[] nums) {
        Deque<Integer> maxq = new ArrayDeque<>();  // indices; values decreasing
        Deque<Integer> minq = new ArrayDeque<>();  // indices; values increasing
        int left = 0;
        long count = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            int x = nums[right];
            while (!maxq.isEmpty() && nums[maxq.peekLast()] <= x) {
                maxq.pollLast();
            }
            maxq.addLast(right);
            while (!minq.isEmpty() && nums[minq.peekLast()] >= x) {
                minq.pollLast();
            }
            minq.addLast(right);
            while (nums[maxq.peekFirst()] - nums[minq.peekFirst()] > 2) {
                left += 1;
                if (maxq.peekFirst() < left) {
                    maxq.pollFirst();
                }
                if (minq.peekFirst() < left) {
                    minq.pollFirst();
                }
            }
            count += right - left + 1;  // every start in [left, right] works
        }
        return count;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If [left, right] is valid, every shorter subarray ending at right is too.
  2. The total can exceed 32 bits.

  • Differences exactly 2.
  • n = 1.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Medium 3413. Maximum Coins From K Consecutive Bags Amazon Array

Problem: Non-overlapping segments [l, r] hold c coins per bag. Collect k consecutive bags (positions up to 10⁹) for the most coins.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: coins = [[8,10,1],[1,3,2],[5,6,4]], k = 4
Output: 10
Explanation: Selecting bags at positions [3, 4, 5, 6] gives the maximum number of coins: 2 + 0 + 4 + 4 = 10.
Example 2
Input: coins = [[1,10,3]], k = 2
Output: 6
Explanation: Selecting bags at positions [1, 2] gives the maximum number of coins: 3 + 3 = 6.

Constraints: 1 ≤ coins.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁹ · coins[i] == [li, ri, ci] · 1 ≤ li ≤ ri ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ ci ≤ 1000 · The given segments are non-overlapping.

Hint 1

Coordinates are up to 10⁹, but there are at most 10⁵ segments. Where can an optimal window start or end?

Hint 2

Try windows starting at each segment's left end (and, mirrored, ending at each right end).

Hint 3

Slide over segments with two pointers, counting full segments and one partial one.

From brute force to the pattern: Sliding over every coordinate is infeasible; aligning windows to segment ends gives O(n log n).

Spot it: Positions are huge, but an optimal window can always be shifted until it starts at a segment's left end or ends at a segment's right end without losing coins. So try windows aligned to segments with a sliding window over segments (full segments summed, one partial), once forwards and once on the mirrored line.

Why not another pattern? Sliding over every position is impossible with coordinates up to 10⁹.

Approach:

  1. best(segs): segments sorted by start; for each segment i, the window is [l_i, l_i + k − 1].
  2. Advance j while segment j ends inside the window, adding its full coins; add the partial overlap of segment j.
  3. Remove segment i when moving on. Run it on the segments and on their mirror images (−r, −l).
class Solution:
    def maximumCoins(self, coins: List[List[int]], k: int) -> int:
        def best(segs):  # windows that start at a segment's left end
            segs.sort()
            res = full = 0
            j = 0
            for i, (l, r, c) in enumerate(segs):
                if j < i:
                    j, full = i, 0  # previous window didn't even cover segment i
                end = l + k - 1
                while j < len(segs) and segs[j][1] <= end:
                    full += (segs[j][1] - segs[j][0] + 1) * segs[j][2]  # segment fully inside
                    j += 1
                partial = 0
                if j < len(segs) and segs[j][0] <= end:
                    partial = (end - segs[j][0] + 1) * segs[j][2]  # cut-off segment at the end
                res = max(res, full + partial)
                if j > i:
                    full -= (r - l + 1) * c  # slide past segment i
            return res

        forward = best([s[:] for s in coins])
        backward = best([[-r, -l, c] for l, r, c in coins])  # windows that end at a right end
        return max(forward, backward)
function maximumCoins(coins: number[][], k: number): number {
    // windows that start at a segment's left end
    function best(segs: number[][]): number {
        segs.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1]);
        let res = 0;
        let full = 0;
        let j = 0;
        for (let i = 0; i < segs.length; i++) {
            const [l, r, c] = segs[i];
            if (j < i) {
                j = i;  // previous window didn't even cover segment i
                full = 0;
            }
            const end = l + k - 1;
            while (j < segs.length && segs[j][1] <= end) {
                full += (segs[j][1] - segs[j][0] + 1) * segs[j][2];  // segment fully inside
                j += 1;
            }
            let partial = 0;
            if (j < segs.length && segs[j][0] <= end) {
                partial = (end - segs[j][0] + 1) * segs[j][2];  // cut-off segment at the end
            }
            res = Math.max(res, full + partial);
            if (j > i) {
                full -= (r - l + 1) * c;  // slide past segment i
            }
        }
        return res;
    }

    const forward = best(coins.map((s) => [...s]));
    const backward = best(coins.map(([l, r, c]) => [-r, -l, c]));  // windows that end at a right end
    return Math.max(forward, backward);
}
class Solution {
    public long maximumCoins(int[][] coins, int k) {
        long[][] forward = new long[coins.length][];
        long[][] backward = new long[coins.length][];
        for (int i = 0; i < coins.length; i++) {
            forward[i] = new long[] {coins[i][0], coins[i][1], coins[i][2]};
            backward[i] = new long[] {-coins[i][1], -coins[i][0], coins[i][2]};  // windows that end at a right end
        }
        return Math.max(best(forward, k), best(backward, k));
    }

    // windows that start at a segment's left end
    private long best(long[][] segs, int k) {
        Arrays.sort(segs, (a, b) -> Long.compare(a[0], b[0]));
        long res = 0;
        long full = 0;
        int j = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < segs.length; i++) {
            long l = segs[i][0], r = segs[i][1], c = segs[i][2];
            if (j < i) {
                j = i;  // previous window didn't even cover segment i
                full = 0;
            }
            long end = l + k - 1;
            while (j < segs.length && segs[j][1] <= end) {
                full += (segs[j][1] - segs[j][0] + 1) * segs[j][2];  // segment fully inside
                j += 1;
            }
            long partial = 0;
            if (j < segs.length && segs[j][0] <= end) {
                partial = (end - segs[j][0] + 1) * segs[j][2];  // cut-off segment at the end
            }
            res = Math.max(res, full + partial);
            if (j > i) {
                full -= (r - l + 1) * c;  // slide past segment i
            }
        }
        return res;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If a window starts inside a gap or mid-segment, shifting it toward the richer side never loses coins until an endpoint aligns; that's why only aligned windows are needed.
  2. Mirroring positions (x → −x) turns "ends at a right end" into "starts at a left end", so one helper handles both.
  3. full holds the coins of segments completely inside the window; at most one segment is cut at the right edge.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k longer than all segments combined.
  • One very long segment (window inside it).
  • Gaps between segments.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

Hard 1703. Minimum Adjacent Swaps for K Consecutive Ones Amazon Array

Problem: Return the fewest adjacent swaps to make k consecutive 1s.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,0,0,1,0,1], k = 2
Output: 1
Explanation: In 1 move, nums could be [1,0,0,0,1,1] and have 2 consecutive 1's.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,0,0,0,0,0,1,1], k = 3
Output: 5
Explanation: In 5 moves, the leftmost 1 can be shifted right until nums = [0,0,0,0,0,1,1,1].

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · nums[i] is 0 or 1. · 1 ≤ k ≤ sum(nums)

Hint 1

Only the positions of the ones matter. Which k ones should end up together?

Hint 2

If you subtract each one's rank from its position, what does "consecutive" become?

Hint 3

Moving points to a common value costs least at the median; use prefix sums for each window.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every window and simulating swaps is O(nk); the median formula is O(n).

Spot it: Choose k consecutive ones (a sliding window over the ones' positions) and gather them together. Gathering into a block is like gathering to one point after the shift q_i = p_i − i; the best meeting point is the median, and prefix sums give the cost of each window in O(1).

Why not another pattern? Simulating swaps for every window is O(n · k) or worse.

Approach:

  1. pos = indices of ones; q[i] = pos[i] − i; prefix sums P of q.
  2. For each window q[i..i+k−1] with median index m = i + k // 2: cost = q[m]·(m − i) − (P[m] − P[i]) + (P[i+k] − P[m+1]) − q[m]·(i + k − m − 1).
  3. Return the minimum.
class Solution:
    def minMoves(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        q = [p - i for i, p in enumerate(i for i, x in enumerate(nums) if x)]  # positions minus rank
        P = [0]
        for v in q:
            P.append(P[-1] + v)
        best = float("inf")
        for i in range(len(q) - k + 1):
            m = i + k // 2  # median of this window
            left = q[m] * (m - i) - (P[m] - P[i])  # pull the left part up to the median
            right = (P[i + k] - P[m + 1]) - q[m] * (i + k - m - 1)  # pull the right part down
            best = min(best, left + right)
        return best
function minMoves(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    // positions of the 1s, minus their rank
    const q: number[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] === 1) {
            q.push(i - q.length);
        }
    }
    const P: number[] = [0];
    for (const v of q) {
        P.push(P[P.length - 1] + v);
    }
    let best = Infinity;
    for (let i = 0; i + k <= q.length; i++) {
        const m = i + Math.floor(k / 2);  // median of this window
        const left = q[m] * (m - i) - (P[m] - P[i]);  // pull the left part up to the median
        const right = (P[i + k] - P[m + 1]) - q[m] * (i + k - m - 1);  // pull the right part down
        best = Math.min(best, left + right);
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int minMoves(int[] nums, int k) {
        // positions of the 1s, minus their rank
        List<Long> q = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            if (nums[i] == 1) {
                q.add((long) i - q.size());
            }
        }
        long[] P = new long[q.size() + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < q.size(); i++) {
            P[i + 1] = P[i] + q.get(i);
        }
        long best = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int i = 0; i + k <= q.size(); i++) {
            int m = i + k / 2;  // median of this window
            long left = q.get(m) * (m - i) - (P[m] - P[i]);  // pull the left part up to the median
            long right = (P[i + k] - P[m + 1]) - q.get(m) * (i + k - m - 1);  // pull the right part down
            best = Math.min(best, left + right);
        }
        return (int) best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Subtracting each one's rank turns "make them consecutive" into "move them all to the same value", which costs Σ|q − target|.
  2. That sum is minimised at the median, and with prefix sums it's computed per window in O(1).
  3. Windows of consecutive ones are optimal: skipping a one in between would only add distance.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 1 → 0.
  • Ones already together → 0.
  • Ones spread far apart.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Hard 2009. Minimum Number of Operations to Make Array Continuous Amazon Array

Problem: Replace elements so the array has distinct values with max − min = n − 1. Return the fewest replacements.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [4,2,5,3]
Output: 0
Explanation: nums is already continuous.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,3,5,6]
Output: 1
Explanation: One possible solution is to change the last element to 4. The resulting array is [1,2,3,5,4], which is continuous.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

The final array is a block of n consecutive values. Which existing values can you keep?

Hint 2

Sort the distinct values and slide a window of width n − 1.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every block start is infeasible; a window over sorted distinct values is O(n log n).

Spot it: The final values are a block [v, v + n − 1]. Keep as many existing distinct values inside some such block as possible: over the sorted distinct values, a sliding window where vals[right] − vals[left] ≤ n − 1.

Why not another pattern? Trying every starting value v up to 10⁹ is impossible.

Approach:

  1. vals = sorted(set(nums)).
  2. For each left, extend right while vals[right] ≤ vals[left] + n − 1.
  3. Answer n − max(window size).
class Solution:
    def minOperations(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        vals = sorted(set(nums))  # duplicates must be replaced anyway
        best = right = 0
        for left in range(len(vals)):
            while right < len(vals) and vals[right] <= vals[left] + n - 1:
                right += 1  # still fits in a block starting at vals[left]
            best = max(best, right - left)  # values we can keep
        return n - best
function minOperations(nums: number[]): number {
    const n = nums.length;
    const vals = [...new Set(nums)].sort((a, b) => a - b);  // duplicates must be replaced anyway
    let best = 0;
    let right = 0;
    for (let left = 0; left < vals.length; left++) {
        while (right < vals.length && vals[right] <= vals[left] + n - 1) {
            right += 1;  // still fits in a block starting at vals[left]
        }
        best = Math.max(best, right - left);  // values we can keep
    }
    return n - best;
}
class Solution {
    public int minOperations(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] vals = Arrays.stream(nums).distinct().sorted().toArray();  // duplicates must be replaced anyway
        int best = 0;
        int right = 0;
        for (int left = 0; left < vals.length; left++) {
            while (right < vals.length && vals[right] <= vals[left] + n - 1) {
                right += 1;  // still fits in a block starting at vals[left]
            }
            best = Math.max(best, right - left);  // values we can keep
        }
        return n - best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Starting the block at an existing value is never worse.
  2. Values kept must be distinct and fit in the block; everything else is replaced.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already continuous → 0.
  • Many duplicates.
  • Values far apart.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 2067. Number of Equal Count Substrings Cisco StringHash Map

Problem: Count substrings in which every letter that appears occurs exactly count times.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: s = "aaabcbbcc", count = 3
Output: 3
Explanation: "aaa", "bcbbcc" and "aaabcbbcc" qualify: each letter in them occurs exactly 3 times.
Example 2
Input: s = "abcd", count = 2
Output: 0
Example 3
Input: s = "a", count = 5
Output: 0

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 3 * 10⁴ · 1 ≤ count ≤ 3 * 10⁴ · s consists only of lowercase English letters

Hint 1

If a valid substring has u distinct letters, how long is it?

Hint 2

For each u, slide a window of that length.

From brute force to the pattern: All substrings with counts: O(26 n²); one fixed window per u: O(26 n).

Spot it: If such a substring has u distinct letters, its length is exactly u · count. So for each u from 1 to 26, a fixed-size sliding window with letter counts, tracking how many letters sit at exactly count.

Why not another pattern? Checking every substring's letter counts is O(26 n²).

Approach:

  1. For u = 1..26: window length L = u · count (skip if > n).
  2. Slide, updating counts and exact = letters with count == count.
  3. When exact == u, the window qualifies.
class Solution:
    def equalCountSubstrings(self, s: str, count: int) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        total = 0
        for u in range(1, 27):  # number of distinct letters in the substring
            L = u * count
            if L > n:
                break
            freq = [0] * 26
            exact = 0  # letters occurring exactly `count` times in the window
            for i, ch in enumerate(s):
                c = ord(ch) - 97
                freq[c] += 1
                if freq[c] == count:
                    exact += 1
                elif freq[c] == count + 1:
                    exact -= 1
                if i >= L:
                    o = ord(s[i - L]) - 97  # character leaving the window
                    if freq[o] == count:
                        exact -= 1
                    freq[o] -= 1
                    if freq[o] == count:
                        exact += 1
                if i >= L - 1 and exact == u:
                    total += 1  # u letters, each exactly count times, fill all L positions
        return total
function equalCountSubstrings(s: string, count: number): number {
    const n = s.length;
    let total = 0;
    for (let u = 1; u <= 26; u++) {  // number of distinct letters in the substring
        const L = u * count;
        if (L > n) {
            break;
        }
        const freq: number[] = new Array(26).fill(0);
        let exact = 0;  // letters occurring exactly `count` times in the window
        for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            const c = s.charCodeAt(i) - 97;
            freq[c] += 1;
            if (freq[c] === count) {
                exact += 1;
            } else if (freq[c] === count + 1) {
                exact -= 1;
            }
            if (i >= L) {
                const o = s.charCodeAt(i - L) - 97;  // character leaving the window
                if (freq[o] === count) {
                    exact -= 1;
                }
                freq[o] -= 1;
                if (freq[o] === count) {
                    exact += 1;
                }
            }
            if (i >= L - 1 && exact === u) {
                total += 1;  // u letters, each exactly count times, fill all L positions
            }
        }
    }
    return total;
}
class Solution {
    public int equalCountSubstrings(String s, int count) {
        int n = s.length();
        int total = 0;
        for (int u = 1; u <= 26; u++) {  // number of distinct letters in the substring
            int L = u * count;
            if (L > n) {
                break;
            }
            int[] freq = new int[26];
            int exact = 0;  // letters occurring exactly `count` times in the window
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                int c = s.charAt(i) - 'a';
                freq[c] += 1;
                if (freq[c] == count) {
                    exact += 1;
                } else if (freq[c] == count + 1) {
                    exact -= 1;
                }
                if (i >= L) {
                    int o = s.charAt(i - L) - 'a';  // character leaving the window
                    if (freq[o] == count) {
                        exact -= 1;
                    }
                    freq[o] -= 1;
                    if (freq[o] == count) {
                        exact += 1;
                    }
                }
                if (i >= L - 1 && exact == u) {
                    total += 1;  // u letters, each exactly count times, fill all L positions
                }
            }
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A window of length u · count with u letters at exactly count has no room for any other letter.
  2. Only the entering and leaving letters change, so each step is O(1).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • count larger than the string → 0.
  • Single letter repeated.
  • All 26 letters.

Complexity: O(26 · n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1208. Get Equal Substrings Within Budget Microsoft String

Problem: Changing s[i] to t[i] costs |s[i] − t[i]|. Return the longest substring you can make equal within maxCost.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abcd", t = "bcdf", maxCost = 3
Output: 3
Explanation: "abc" of s can change to "bcd". That costs 3, so the maximum length is 3.
Example 2
Input: s = "abcd", t = "cdef", maxCost = 3
Output: 1
Explanation: Each character in s costs 2 to change to character in t, so the maximum length is 1.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · t.length == s.length · 0 ≤ maxCost ≤ 10⁶ · s and t consist of only lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Turn the problem into an array of costs.

Hint 2

Longest subarray with sum ≤ maxCost: sliding window.

From brute force to the pattern: All substrings: O(n²); sliding window: O(n).

Spot it: Costs are non-negative, so a longer window never costs less → variable sliding window.

Why not another pattern? Checking every substring is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Extend right, adding its cost.
  2. While the total exceeds maxCost, remove left's cost and move left.
  3. Track the longest window.
class Solution:
    def equalSubstring(self, s: str, t: str, maxCost: int) -> int:
        left = total = best = 0
        for right in range(len(s)):
            total += abs(ord(s[right]) - ord(t[right]))
            while total > maxCost:
                total -= abs(ord(s[left]) - ord(t[left]))  # shrink from the left
                left += 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best
function equalSubstring(s: string, t: string, maxCost: number): number {
    let left = 0;
    let total = 0;
    let best = 0;
    for (let right = 0; right < s.length; right++) {
        total += Math.abs(s.charCodeAt(right) - t.charCodeAt(right));
        while (total > maxCost) {
            total -= Math.abs(s.charCodeAt(left) - t.charCodeAt(left));  // shrink from the left
            left += 1;
        }
        best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int equalSubstring(String s, String t, int maxCost) {
        int left = 0;
        int total = 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            total += Math.abs(s.charAt(right) - t.charAt(right));
            while (total > maxCost) {
                total -= Math.abs(s.charAt(left) - t.charAt(left));  // shrink from the left
                left += 1;
            }
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Non-negative costs make the window monotone.
  2. Each index enters and leaves once.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • maxCost = 0 (only equal characters).
  • Everything affordable.
  • Nothing affordable → 0.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Hard 220. Contains Duplicate III Netflix ArrayHash Map

Problem: Return whether two indices i ≠ j exist with |i − j| ≤ indexDiff and |nums[i] − nums[j]| ≤ valueDiff.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,1], indexDiff = 3, valueDiff = 0
Output: true
Explanation: We can choose (i, j) = (0, 3). We satisfy the three conditions: i != j --> 0 != 3 abs(i - j) <= indexDiff --> abs(0 - 3) <= 3 abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) <= valueDiff --> abs(1 - 1) <= 0
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,5,9,1,5,9], indexDiff = 2, valueDiff = 3
Output: false
Explanation: After trying all the possible pairs (i, j), we cannot satisfy the three conditions, so we return false.

Constraints: 2 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · -10⁹ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ indexDiff ≤ nums.length · 0 ≤ valueDiff ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

The index condition is a sliding window.

Hint 2

Group values into buckets of width valueDiff + 1. Where can a close value be?

From brute force to the pattern: Check all pairs within indexDiff: O(n · indexDiff); buckets make it O(n).

Spot it: The index limit is a sliding window of the last indexDiff values. To find a close value inside it in O(1), put values into buckets of width valueDiff + 1 (a hash map bucket → value): two values in one bucket are close, and a match can otherwise only be in a neighbouring bucket.

Why not another pattern? Comparing each value with the whole window is O(n · indexDiff); a sorted container works in O(n log k) but buckets are O(n).

Approach:

  1. w = valueDiff + 1; bucket id x // w (floor division handles negatives).
  2. For each value: if its bucket is occupied → true; if a neighbouring bucket holds a value within valueDiff → true.
  3. Store the value in its bucket; drop nums[i − indexDiff]'s bucket so the window stays indexDiff wide.
class Solution:
    def containsNearbyAlmostDuplicate(self, nums: List[int], indexDiff: int, valueDiff: int) -> bool:
        width = valueDiff + 1  # any two values in one bucket differ by at most valueDiff
        buckets = {}  # bucket id -> the value in the window that falls there
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            b = x // width
            if b in buckets:
                return True
            if b - 1 in buckets and x - buckets[b - 1] <= valueDiff:
                return True
            if b + 1 in buckets and buckets[b + 1] - x <= valueDiff:
                return True
            buckets[b] = x
            if i >= indexDiff:
                del buckets[nums[i - indexDiff] // width]  # slide the window: that index is now too far back
        return False
function containsNearbyAlmostDuplicate(nums: number[], indexDiff: number, valueDiff: number): boolean {
    const width = valueDiff + 1;  // any two values in one bucket differ by at most valueDiff
    const buckets = new Map<number, number>();  // bucket id -> the value in the window that falls there
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        const x = nums[i];
        const b = Math.floor(x / width);  // floor, so negative values get their own buckets too
        if (buckets.has(b)) {
            return true;
        }
        if (buckets.has(b - 1) && x - buckets.get(b - 1)! <= valueDiff) {
            return true;
        }
        if (buckets.has(b + 1) && buckets.get(b + 1)! - x <= valueDiff) {
            return true;
        }
        buckets.set(b, x);
        if (i >= indexDiff) {
            buckets.delete(Math.floor(nums[i - indexDiff] / width));  // slide the window: that index is now too far back
        }
    }
    return false;
}
class Solution {
    public boolean containsNearbyAlmostDuplicate(int[] nums, int indexDiff, int valueDiff) {
        long width = (long) valueDiff + 1;  // any two values in one bucket differ by at most valueDiff
        Map<Long, Long> buckets = new HashMap<>();  // bucket id -> the value in the window that falls there
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            long x = nums[i];
            long b = Math.floorDiv(x, width);  // floor, so negative values get their own buckets too
            if (buckets.containsKey(b)) {
                return true;
            }
            if (buckets.containsKey(b - 1) && x - buckets.get(b - 1) <= valueDiff) {
                return true;
            }
            if (buckets.containsKey(b + 1) && buckets.get(b + 1) - x <= valueDiff) {
                return true;
            }
            buckets.put(b, x);
            if (i >= indexDiff) {
                buckets.remove(Math.floorDiv((long) nums[i - indexDiff], width));  // slide the window: that index is now too far back
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each bucket holds at most one value: a second one would already have returned true.
  2. A close value is either in the same bucket or in a neighbour; anything two buckets away differs by more than valueDiff.
  3. Removing the value from indexDiff positions back keeps only indices within range.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • valueDiff = 0 (exact duplicates).
  • Negative numbers (floor division).
  • indexDiff ≥ n.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(min(n, indexDiff)) space.
